lessons.title: Introduction to Output
lessons.summary: We have previously used print() to display a single value or variable. Here's a quick recap:

blocks.content: We have previously used print() to display a single value or variable. Here's a quick recap:

blocks.code:
# Print an integer
print(34) # Output: 34
# Print a string
print("Squid Game") # Output: Squid Game
# Create a variable
city = "London"
# Print the city variable
print(city) # Output: London
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.content: Now, you'll learn how to print multiple values and variables. You'll also explore f-strings, which makes it easier to print multiple data in the desired format.

lessons.title: Print Multiple Values
lessons.summary: We can print multiple pieces of data at once by separating them with commas. For example:

blocks.content: We can print multiple pieces of data at once by separating them with commas. For example:

blocks.code:
# Display three numbers
print(67, -5, 19)
# Display two strings
print("Hey.", "Are you enjoying the course?")
# Display numbers and strings
print("Rating:", 8.5)
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.code:
Hey. Are you enjoying the course?
Rating: 8.5
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.content: Here, the comma is used for separation and is not printed.
Additionally, spaces before or after the comma don't affect the output. By default, print() always inserts a single space between the values.

instructions.content:
Print a String and a Number

Write a program to print a string and a number using a single print() function.

objectives: Define a variable age with value 19.
Create another variable message to store the string "My age is:".
Use a single print() function to display the message and age variables together.

age = 19
# Create the message variable

# Print message and age variables

blocks.caption: Solution

blocks.title: AI Explanation
blocks.context:
You're becoming a coding whiz! Here's how it works:

First up, we have an age variable, storing the number 19. Imagine it as your handy virtual sticky note, holding the data tight.

Next, the string "My age is:" gets wrapped in a message variable, like saving your favorite quote in a treasure chest.

Finally, we make magic happen with the print function. It joins message and age, weaving them into a statement: "My age is: 19".

Now, isn't that a neat way to display your age to the virtual world? Feel ready to age up your skills and tackle some new coding challenges?

lessons.summary: It's possible to use a single print() function to display output in multiple lines.

blocks.content: It's possible to use a single print() function to display output in multiple lines.
To do this, we use the newline character \n in the position where we want to break the line:
Every use of \n adds a newline. So, if we use another \n, it will add a space between the separated lines.

lessons.title: Print Variables Using f-strings
lessons.summary: To print variables using f-strings, you need to wrap them inside curly braces {}.

blocks.content: To print variables using f-strings, you need to wrap them inside curly braces {}.
For example:

name = "Alice"
location = "Wonderland"
print(f"My name is {name} and I live in {location}.")

Why did the string cross the function? To get concatenated! 🌟 Here's how it works:

In this coding exercise, we're playing with strings. We're using the print() function to display a beautifully formatted sentence.

The code uses f-string formatting, a Python feature that allows us to easily insert variables into a string. All you need are curly braces and a dream!

The variables title and author hold specific text values, which, in this case, are book details. Once fed into the f-string, they transform into a coherent sentence.

As a result, the output will be: "The Great Gatsby by Fitzgerald." Isn't it elegant how a few simple lines can convey so much?

lessons.title: Common Mistakes (I)
lessons.summary: Before moving to the next lesson, let's discuss common mistakes beginners may make.

blocks.content: Before moving to the next lesson, let's discuss common mistakes beginners may make.
1. Spelling Error
This one is obvious—using wrong variable names and misspelling words will cause an error. For example:

blocks.code:
annual_income = 95000
# error because of a spelling mistake
print(annual_icome)
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.code: NameError: name 'annual_icome' is not defined. Did you mean: 'annual_income'?
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.content: In most cases, carefully reading the error message helps us fix these problems easily.
For instance, the output clearly states that annual_icome is not defined in line 4.
Also, Python is case-sensitive. So annual_income and Annual_income are also not the same.
The same rule applies to print() as well—writing it as Print() or any other way will result in an error.
2. Adding Spaces at the Beginning
In Python, indentation has a specific meaning. So, if we add unnecessary spaces at the beginning, we will get an error. For example,
If you run the program, you will get an error because there are spaces before print().

lessons.title: Common Mistakes (II)
lessons.summary: We have seen many beginners make this mistake. They usually forget to close the string with quotation marks. For example,

blocks.content: We have seen many beginners make this mistake. They usually forget to close the string with quotation marks. For example,
Here, Python doesn't understand what "Hello is.
"Hello is not a string because it doesn't have the closing quotation mark. And it's not a variable because we cannot use quotation marks in variable names.

blocks.text: 4. Forgetting Commas in the print() Function

blocks.content: Here, Python interprets "Age:" age as a single item. Since it's neither a string nor a variable, we get an error.

blocks.text: 5. Forgetting to use f in a f-string

blocks.content: If you forget to include f before the quotation marks, the string is treated as a normal string. As a result, {age} is interpreted as plain text instead of being evaluated as a variable.
Avoid these five common mistakes and enjoy a smoother programming experience.
You can improve your Python skills by practicing regularly and staying mindful of common mistakes. To learn more about printing in Python, check out the Printing Basics in Python article.
